newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Call Luther Vandross Love Balladeer, not Doctor Love.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Call Luther Vandross Love Balladeer, not Doctor Love.

text.p: Luther Vandross' name, to many, is synonymous with love songs. That is cool with him.
But do not call him "The Love Doctor" or "Loverman" Luther. Bad Move.
"When I'm on a TV show, and somebody introduces me with, 'We'll be right back with The Love Doctor, Luther Vandross,' it makes me mad," he told Reuters. "It really is not flattering to me."

It is not hard to see how he got the label. Since his debut in 1980, the New York native has sold more than 15 million albums by manifesting emotions and affections in his gifted tenor, singing introspective ballads like "A House Is Not a Home," "There's Nothing Better Than Love," and "Here and Now."

"Your Secret Love," his newest CD, delivers 12 more cuts of Vandross' uniquely stirring soul, delving into relationships that survive, "Whether Or Not The World Gets Better," and those that fail, when "Love Don't Love You Anymore."

That is where he connects with his audience, he says -- in their hearts, not, er, elsewhere on the anatomy. "I've never once sung about making love. I don't do it. I sing about being in love," he said. "I sing about the things that emotionally scar you to the degree that you are unable to get out of bed and start your day, because your emotions and things that burden you are heavy."

His music backs up his argument. Where others may talk about love like a commodity or a means to an end, Vandross' modus operandi is that of a good friend, with a great voice, who speaks to your joy or pain from his own experience.

Still, he says, the title is hard to shake. "People try to lump all black male singers into Barry White-land, into that whole bedroom world," he said. "But that's not what I do. I want to be remembered as one of the premier singers of our time, not as the 'Love Doctor' or the 'Master of Bedroom Music.'"

Sometimes even his friends help perpetuate the problem. Arsenio Hall, in the notes accompanying Vandross' 1986 greatest hits package "The Best of Love," wrote that if were he stuck on a deserted island with the discs, "I hope that I'm stranded with a woman. The effect Luther's music has on women is incredible! Just trust me!"

"And what kills me," Vandross said with a chuckle, "is when (younger performers) come out on stage, pumping the pelvis, singing a thousand notes a minute, and when the host asks, 'Who inspired you?', they say 'Luther!' And I say, 'What? I never did any of the stuff that you just did!'"

Despite the misunderstanding, Vandross says he does not plan to change the flavor of his music for any reason. After making an album of covers ("Songs") and a Christmas album since his last original release in 1993, he welcomed the chance to reunite with long-time collaborators Marcus Miller, Skip Anderson and Nat Adderly Jr. to do what he called "a real Luther album."

"Your Secret Love" finds Vandross wrapped in his familiar mid-tempo glow. His unique voice is still as strikingly clear as his grooves are infectious. And he reassembles his all-star team of background singers -- led by Cissy Houston, Lisa Fischer, and Cindy Mizelle -- whose tight, powerful harmonies fill the spaces in-between and often colour the foreground.

Vandross also turns in an exhilarating treatment of the Imperials' classic, "Goin' out of my head," a song whose crescendo would frighten less capable artists. And no self-respecting "Loverman" would be caught dead pleading, "I want you to want me/I need you to need me..."

His true fans know what to expect from him. Most often, they call him 'Luther,' not Loverman or Mr. Vandross, probably because his songs have endeared him to them or because they have brought them closer to another loved one.
And he is cool with that. "When people ask if I'm always going to sing love songs, my answer is always, 'Hell yes.'"
